# TI-LFA over SR-MPLS: Computing Repair Lists and Label Stacks

The previous chapter introduced Topology Independent Loop-Free Alternate (TI-LFA), P-space, Q-space and repair lists. This chapter does the computation. You will build the shortest-path trees a Point of Local Repair (PLR) builds, find the P and Q nodes on the post-convergence path, turn the result into an SR-MPLS label stack, and check it against the platform's Maximum SID Depth (MSD). The lab is a small standard-library Python program. It reproduces both worked examples in RFC 9855 and then measures how much classic LFA, remote LFA and TI-LFA cover on rings and on a meshed core.

Doing this by hand once pays off in operations. When a router reports a backup path with three labels you can check it is the one you expect. When a platform warns that some prefixes are unprotected because the repair exceeds MSD you will know which topologies cause it. And when a vendor's "show" output disagrees with your mental model you will have a reference to compare against.

## Learning goals

- Compute P-space, extended P-space and Q-space for a link or node failure, including the strict treatment of equal-cost paths.
- Find the expected post-convergence path and pick the P and Q nodes on it.
- Express a repair as a repair list (RL) in each of the four RFC 9855 forms, from empty to Node-SID plus Adj-SIDs.
- Turn an RL into SR-MPLS labels with an SRGB and Adj-SIDs, and apply the RFC 9855 section 7.1 rules for the active segment and penultimate-hop popping (PHP).
- Compare LFA, remote LFA and TI-LFA coverage on a topology, and spot repairs that exceed MSD.
- Read FRR's TI-LFA configuration and backup-route output with that model in mind.

## Version note

Everything in the lab ran on the book's build box with Python 3.13.5 (standard library only), as an unprivileged user. No routers or MPLS data plane are involved; the program models the control-plane computation a PLR does. The FRR configuration near the end is written from the FRR `isisd` and `ospfd` documentation and is **not run here**. Check the documentation for your FRR version before using it, because SR and TI-LFA options have changed between releases.

## The computation in one page

A PLR S protects a resource X: a link S-F, a neighbour node F, or a shared-risk link group. For every destination D whose primary path uses X, S precomputes what to do in the moment X fails, before the IGP has reconverged. TI-LFA's answer is to send the packet along the path the network will use *after* convergence, and to add just enough segments that no router on the way loops the packet back toward X while the rest of the network still has the old topology.

The steps, following RFC 9855 sections 4 and 5:

1. **Post-convergence path.** Run SPF from S on the topology with X removed. Pick the path to D. This is where traffic will go anyway once the IGP converges, so repairing onto it avoids a second path change.
2. **P-space.** P(S, X) is the set of nodes S reaches on its *pre-failure* shortest paths without any of those paths, including equal-cost splits, crossing X. Sending a packet to a P node with that node's Node-SID is safe: every router on the way still uses old shortest paths, and none of them cross X.
3. **Extended P-space.** P'(S, X) is the union of the P-spaces of S's neighbours that are not reached through X. S can hand the packet to such a neighbour directly, so the neighbour's view counts. RFC 9855 section 4.1 restricts this to neighbours on the post-convergence path.
4. **Q-space.** Q(D, X) is the set of nodes whose shortest paths *to D* do not cross X. Once a packet reaches a Q node, plain shortest-path forwarding toward D is safe.
5. **Pick P and Q.** Intersect both sets with the post-convergence path. Take P as the deepest P node along the path and Q as the first Q node at or after P.
6. **Build the RL.** If P is Q, one Node-SID (or nothing at all if P is the next hop). If P and Q are adjacent, Node-SID(P) plus Adj-SID(P-Q). If they are further apart, Node-SID(P) plus Adj-SIDs along the path to Q. RFC 9855 leaves shorter encodings of the P-to-Q stretch to implementations (section 5.4).

The four repair forms match the four subsections of RFC 9855 section 5:

| Form | When | RL | Older technique it resembles |
|------|------|----|------------------------------|
| Direct neighbour | next hop on the post-convergence path is in P' and Q | empty | post-convergence LFA |
| PQ node | a remote node is in both P' and Q | Node-SID(PQ) | remote LFA tunnel |
| P and Q adjacent | P and Q are neighbours on the path | Node-SID(P), Adj-SID(P-Q) | directed LFA (DLFA) |
| Distant P and Q | gap between P and Q | Node-SID(P), Adj-SIDs to Q | none: this is what only SR can express |

```text
 PLR S                 post-convergence path                       D
   o-----o-----o-------o=========o=========o-------o-----o
         ^             ^                   ^
         |             P (deepest node     Q (first node whose
         |               S can reach on      own path to D avoids X)
     next hop            old paths)
                 <-- Node-SID(P) -->< Adj-SIDs P..Q ><-- shortest path -->
```

Two properties make this "topology independent". First, the RL can always be built if the post-convergence path exists, because Adj-SIDs can pin every hop if needed. Second, the repair follows the post-convergence path, so when the IGP converges the traffic does not move again.

## From a repair list to labels

On SR-MPLS (RFC 8660), segments become labels:

- A **Node-SID** is advertised as an index. Each router turns it into a label by adding the index to its own Segment Routing Global Block (SRGB) base. With the same SRGB everywhere (the common and recommended deployment), Node-SID index 5 is label 16005 on every router when the SRGB starts at 16000.
- An **Adj-SID** is a local label that means "pop and send out of this specific adjacency". It is only meaningful on the router that allocated it. The lab gives each node its own block (24100s for the first node, 24200s for the second and so on) so you can see whose label is whose.

The packet arriving at S already carries an *active segment*, typically Node-SID(D). RFC 9855 section 7.1 says what to do with it:

1. If the active segment is a Node-SID signalled with PHP, and the RL ends with an Adj-SID that terminates on D's penultimate node, **pop** the active segment. The last Adj-SID delivers the packet to the router that would have popped it anyway.
2. Otherwise **pop and re-push** the active segment using the label value in Q's SRGB, then push the RL on top. With a uniform SRGB the value does not change.

So the label depth on the repaired packet is the RL length plus zero or one. That depth is what has to fit the MSD the PLR can push, which routers advertise in the IGP (RFC 8491 for IS-IS, RFC 8476 for OSPF). Most routers push only a handful of labels at line rate, so the RL length is an operational constraint, not just an elegance metric. RFC 9855 section 3 makes the point directly: an RL made only of Adj-SIDs always works but can be too long for hardware.

## The lab

Three files. `tilfa.py` is the model: a topology class with ECMP-aware Dijkstra, the P/Q-space computations, the RL builder and the label rules. `rfc-figures.py` reproduces RFC 9855 Figures 1 and 2. `coverage.py` runs every PLR against every destination on four topologies, with link protection of the primary next hop.

The model makes these simplifications, all stated in the code: metrics are symmetric (so the reverse SPF for Q-space equals a forward SPF from D), one path is picked deterministically when the post-convergence path has equal-cost options, the SRGB is uniform, and SRLGs are not modelled.

```{.python filename="tilfa.py"}
"""TI-LFA (RFC 9855) repair lists over SR-MPLS (RFC 8660), computed from a link-state graph.
Standard library only. Metrics are symmetric unless a topology says otherwise."""
import heapq, itertools

class Topo:
    def __init__(self, links, srgb_base=16000):
        self.adj = {}
        for a, b, m in links:
            self.adj.setdefault(a, {})[b] = m
            self.adj.setdefault(b, {})[a] = m
        self.nodes = sorted(self.adj)
        self.index = {n: i + 1 for i, n in enumerate(self.nodes)}      # prefix-SID index per node
        self.srgb = srgb_base
        # Adj-SIDs are local labels; give each node its own block for readability
        self.adj_sid = {}
        for i, n in enumerate(self.nodes):
            for j, nb in enumerate(sorted(self.adj[n])):
                self.adj_sid[(n, nb)] = 24000 + 100 * (i + 1) + j

    def node_label(self, n):
        return self.srgb + self.index[n]

    def spf(self, root, x=None):
        """Dijkstra with ECMP predecessors. x = ('link', a, b) or ('node', n) is removed."""
        dist, preds, heap = {root: 0}, {root: set()}, [(0, root)]
        while heap:
            d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
            if d > dist[u]:
                continue
            for v, m in self.adj[u].items():
                if x and (x[0] == "node" and v == x[1] or x[0] == "link" and {u, v} == {x[1], x[2]}):
                    continue
                nd = d + m
                if nd < dist.get(v, float("inf")):
                    dist[v], preds[v] = nd, {u}
                    heapq.heappush(heap, (nd, v))
                elif nd == dist[v]:
                    preds[v].add(u)
        return dist, preds

    def clean_set(self, root, x):
        """Nodes reachable from root on pre-failure shortest paths, with no ECMP branch through x."""
        dist, preds = self.spf(root)
        tainted = {}
        for v in sorted(dist, key=dist.get):
            if v == root:
                tainted[v] = False
                continue
            t = False
            for p in preds[v]:
                if tainted[p] or (x[0] == "link" and {p, v} == {x[1], x[2]}) or (x[0] == "node" and p == x[1]):
                    t = True
            if x[0] == "node" and v == x[1]:
                t = True
            tainted[v] = t
        return {v for v, t in tainted.items() if not t}

    def p_space(self, s, x):
        return self.clean_set(s, x)

    def ext_p_space(self, s, x, on_path=None):
        """P'(S,X): union of P(N,X) for neighbors N not reached through X (RFC 9855 s2.1, s4.1)."""
        out = set(self.p_space(s, x))
        for n in self.adj[s]:
            if x[0] == "node" and n == x[1] or x[0] == "link" and {s, n} == {x[1], x[2]}:
                continue
            if on_path is not None and n not in on_path:
                continue
            out |= self.clean_set(n, x)
        return out

    def q_space(self, d, x):
        # symmetric metrics: reverse SPF from D equals forward SPF from D
        return self.clean_set(d, x)

    def path(self, s, d, x=None):
        dist, preds = self.spf(s, x)
        if d not in dist:
            return None, None
        hops, v = [d], d
        while v != s:
            v = min(preds[v])            # deterministic tie-break: lowest name
            hops.append(v)
        return hops[::-1], dist[d]

    def repair(self, s, d, x):
        """Return dict describing the TI-LFA repair at PLR s for destination d when x fails."""
        pc, cost = self.path(s, d, x)
        if pc is None:
            return None
        P = self.ext_p_space(s, x, on_path=set(pc))
        Q = self.q_space(d, x)
        p_idx = max(i for i, n in enumerate(pc) if n in P)
        q_idx = next(i for i in range(p_idx, len(pc)) if pc[i] in Q)
        p, q = pc[p_idx], pc[q_idx]
        segs = []
        if p == d:
            pass                                       # D itself is reachable loop-free: the active segment suffices
        elif p_idx > 1:                                  # P is not the first hop: steer to it with its Node-SID
            segs.append(("node", p))
        for a, b in zip(pc[p_idx:q_idx], pc[p_idx + 1:q_idx + 1]) if p != d else ():
            segs.append(("adj", a, b))
        kind = ("empty RL (post-convergence next hop already loop-free)" if not segs else
                "PQ node (one Node-SID)" if p == q else
                "P and Q adjacent (Node-SID + Adj-SID)" if q_idx - p_idx == 1 and p_idx > 1 else
                "Adj-SIDs from P to Q")
        return dict(pc=pc, cost=cost, P=sorted(P & set(pc)), Q=sorted(Q & set(pc)), p=p, q=q,
                    segs=segs, nexthop=pc[1], kind=kind)

    def labels(self, r, d, php=True):
        """SR-MPLS labels on the repaired packet, top first, for active segment Node-SID(d) (RFC 9855 s7.1)."""
        stack = [self.node_label(s[1]) if s[0] == "node" else self.adj_sid[(s[1], s[2])] for s in r["segs"]]
        q, segs = r["q"], r["segs"]
        if segs and q == d:
            return stack                      # the repair itself delivers to D
        if not segs:
            # only the active segment, swapped toward the repair next hop; popped if that hop is D (PHP)
            return [] if php and r["nexthop"] == d else [self.node_label(d)]
        q_path = self.path(q, d)[0]
        if php and segs[-1][0] == "adj" and len(q_path) == 2:
            return stack                      # rule 1: Q is D's penultimate hop, active segment popped
        return stack + [self.node_label(d)]   # rule 2: re-push Node-SID(D) per Q's SRGB (homogeneous here)

def fmt_seg(t, s):
    return f"Node-SID({s[1]})={t.node_label(s[1])}" if s[0] == "node" else f"Adj-SID({s[1]}-{s[2]})={t.adj_sid[(s[1], s[2])]}"

def lfa_ok(t, s, d, f):
    """RFC 5286 link-protecting LFA: some neighbor N != F with dist(N,D) < dist(N,S) + dist(S,D)."""
    ds = t.spf(s)[0]
    for n in t.adj[s]:
        if n == f:
            continue
        dn = t.spf(n)[0]
        if dn[d] < dn[s] + ds[d]:
            # and N's own shortest path must not use S-F (guaranteed by the inequality for link protection)
            return True
    return False

def rlfa_ok(t, s, d, x):
    """RFC 7490 remote LFA: a PQ node exists (extended P-space of S intersect Q-space of D)."""
    return bool(t.ext_p_space(s, x) & t.q_space(d, x))
```

The P-space test is the part to read closely. `clean_set` walks the shortest-path DAG from the root in distance order and marks a node tainted if *any* predecessor on *any* equal-cost path is tainted, is the failed node, or reaches it over the failed link. That is the strict definition: a node with one clean path and one equal-cost path through X is not in P-space, because the routers on the way may hash the packet onto the bad branch.

```{.python filename="rfc-figures.py"}
"""Reproduce the two worked examples in RFC 9855 (Figures 1 and 2)."""
from tilfa import Topo, fmt_seg

K = 1000
fig1 = Topo([("S", "N1", 1), ("N1", "D", 1), ("S", "N2", 1), ("S", "N3", K), ("N1", "R1", 1),
             ("N1", "R2", 1), ("D", "R3", 1), ("N2", "R1", 1), ("R1", "R2", K), ("R2", "R3", K), ("N3", "R1", K)])
x = ("node", "N1")
print("== RFC 9855 Figure 1: PLR S, destination D, protect node N1")
print("  P(S,N1)            =", sorted(fig1.p_space("S", x) - {"S"}), " strict: S->R1 has an ECMP branch via N1")
print("  P'(S,N1) extended  =", sorted(fig1.ext_p_space("S", x) - {"S", "N1"}), " R1 enters via neighbor N2")
print("  Q(D,N1)            =", sorted(fig1.q_space("D", x) - {"D"}))
r = fig1.repair("S", "D", x)
print("  post-convergence   =", " -> ".join(r["pc"]), f"(cost {r['cost']})")
print("  P on path / Q on path =", r["P"], "/", r["Q"], f"-> P={r['p']} Q={r['q']}")
print("  repair list        =", ", ".join(fmt_seg(fig1, s) for s in r["segs"]), f"| out via {r['nexthop']}")
print("  label stack (PHP)  =", fig1.labels(r, "D", php=True), " top first")
print("  label stack (no PHP)=", fig1.labels(r, "D", php=False))

fig2 = Topo([("S", "R2", 1), ("R2", "R3", 1), ("R3", "R4", 1), ("R4", "R5", 1), ("R5", "D", 1),
             ("R2", "R7", K), ("R3", "R7", 1), ("R3", "R8", 1), ("R7", "R8", K), ("R8", "R4", K),
             ("R7", "R9", K), ("R9", "R10", 1), ("R8", "R10", 1)])
x = ("node", "R3")
print("\n== RFC 9855 Figure 2: PLR R2, destination D, protect node R3")
r = fig2.repair("R2", "D", x)
print("  post-convergence   =", " -> ".join(r["pc"]), f"(cost {r['cost']})")
print("  P on path / Q on path =", r["P"], "/", r["Q"], f"-> P={r['p']} Q={r['q']}")
print("  repair list        =", ", ".join(fmt_seg(fig2, s) for s in r["segs"]), f"| out via {r['nexthop']}")
print("  label stack (PHP)  =", fig2.labels(r, "D", php=True), " top first")
```

```text
  repair list        = Node-SID(R1)=16005, Adj-SID(R1-R2)=24503, Adj-SID(R2-R3)=24602 | out via N2
```

### Figure 1: node protection with distant P and Q

RFC 9855 Figure 1 (metric 1 except the starred links at 1000):

```text
     S --------- N1 --------- D
     *\          | \          |
     * \         |  \         |
     *  \        |   \        |
     *   N2----- R1***R2 *** R3
     *           *
     N3 **********
```

S protects traffic to D against the failure of node N1. The post-convergence path is S, N2, R1, R2, R3, D at cost 2003: the only way around N1 uses the two expensive links R1-R2 and R2-R3.

The first output line is worth stopping on. The RFC text says P(S, N1) is [N3, N2, R1]. The program says [N2, N3] and puts R1 only in the *extended* P-space. Both paths S-N1-R1 and S-N2-R1 cost 2, so S's shortest paths to R1 include an equal-cost split through N1, and the RFC's own definition ("without any of those paths (including equal-cost path splits) transiting through X") excludes R1. R1 is still usable as the P node, because S can hand the packet to its neighbour N2 and N2's only shortest path to R1 is the direct link. That is exactly why the extended P-space exists. The repair list comes out the same as the RFC's: `Node-SID(R1)`, `Adj-SID(R1-R2)`, `Adj-SID(R2-R3)`, sent out via N2.

Why the Adj-SIDs? R2 is not in Q-space: its shortest path to D goes R2-N1-D at cost 2. If the packet arrived at R2 with only Node-SID(D) on it, R2 would send it straight back toward the failed N1. Only R3 is in Q(D, N1). So the RL has to pin both expensive links.

The two label lines show RFC 9855 section 7.1 in action. R3 is D's penultimate hop, and the RL ends with an Adj-SID into R3. With PHP, rule 1 applies: the active segment (16001, D's label) is popped and not re-pushed, so the repaired packet carries three labels. If D's Node-SID was advertised with the no-PHP flag, rule 2 applies and D's label goes back on the bottom: four labels.

### Figure 2: the P node is the next hop

RFC 9855 Figure 2 (metric 1 except R2-R7, R7-R8, R8-R4 and R7-R9 at 1000):

```text
     S --- R2 --- R3 ---- R4 --- R5 --- D
              *   |  \   *
                * |   \ *
                 R7 ** R8
                  *    |
                  *    |
                 R9 -- R10
```

R2 protects traffic for D against the failure of R3. The post-convergence path is R2, R7, R8, R4, R5, D. R7 is the deepest P node, and it is R2's own next hop, so no Node-SID is needed to reach it. Q is R4. The RL is two Adj-SIDs, `Adj-SID(R7-R8)` and `Adj-SID(R8-R4)`, out via R7, which is exactly the RFC's answer. R4 is not D's penultimate hop (R5 is), so rule 2 applies and D's label 16001 is re-pushed under the RL: three labels.

RFC 9855 uses this figure for a different warning (section 9). If the Adj-SID for R7-R8 is itself *protected*, and R7-R8 fails during the repair, R7 applies its own repair and the packet gets a second RL. Implementations may prefer unprotected Adj-SIDs in RLs to avoid such double FRR. Fast reroute is for one planned failure. When more fails at once, IGP convergence speed is what saves you.

### Coverage: LFA, remote LFA and TI-LFA

```{.python filename="coverage.py"}
"""Coverage of LFA vs remote LFA vs TI-LFA for every PLR, every protected link, every destination."""
import collections
from tilfa import Topo, fmt_seg, lfa_ok, rlfa_ok

def survey(name, t, msd):
    cases = lfa = rlfa = ti = 0
    sizes, over, adj_only = collections.Counter(), [], 0
    for s in t.nodes:
        for d in t.nodes:
            if d == s:
                continue
            pc, _ = t.path(s, d)
            f = pc[1]                                   # primary next hop
            x = ("link", s, f)
            r = t.repair(s, d, x)
            if r is None:
                continue
            cases += 1
            lfa += lfa_ok(t, s, d, f)
            rlfa += lfa_ok(t, s, d, f) or rlfa_ok(t, s, d, x)
            ti += 1
            st = t.labels(r, d)
            sizes[len(st)] += 1
            adj_only = max(adj_only, len(r["pc"]) - 1)     # an Adj-SID for every post-convergence hop
            if len(st) > msd:
                over.append((s, d, f, r, st))
    pct = lambda n: f"{n}/{cases} ({100 * n / cases:.0f}%)"
    print(f"== {name}: {len(t.nodes)} nodes, link protection, {cases} (PLR, destination) pairs")
    print(f"  LFA (RFC 5286)        {pct(lfa)}")
    print(f"  LFA + remote LFA      {pct(rlfa)}")
    print(f"  TI-LFA (RFC 9855)     {pct(ti)}")
    print("  SR labels on the repaired packet:",
          ", ".join(f"{k} labels: {v}" for k, v in sorted(sizes.items())))
    for s, d, f, r, st in over[:3]:
        print(f"  over MSD {msd}: PLR {s} -> {d}, link {s}-{f}: {len(st)} labels {st} via",
              " -> ".join(r["pc"]))
    print(f"  pairs over MSD {msd}: {len(over)}  (deepest TI-LFA stack {max(sizes)}; Adj-SID-only would need up to {adj_only})")

# 1. A plain ring: the classic LFA failure case
ring = Topo([(a, b, 10) for a, b in zip("ABCDEF", "BCDEFA")])
survey("6-node ring, all metrics 10", ring, msd=3)

# 2. The same ring with one expensive link, as you get with a long-haul or a costed-out span
ring2 = Topo([(a, b, 10) for a, b in zip("ABCDEF", "BCDEF")] + [("F", "A", 100)])
survey("6-node ring, F-A metric 100", ring2, msd=3)

# 3. Ring of 8 with one costly span: repairs get deeper
ring8 = Topo([(a, b, 10) for a, b in zip("ABCDEFGH", "BCDEFGH")] + [("H", "A", 100)])
survey("8-node ring, H-A metric 100", ring8, msd=2)

# 4. A small two-plane core with a costed cross-link (well meshed)
core = Topo([("P1", "P2", 10), ("P2", "P3", 10), ("P3", "P4", 10), ("P4", "P1", 10), ("P1", "P3", 15),
             ("PE1", "P1", 10), ("PE1", "P2", 10), ("PE2", "P3", 10), ("PE2", "P4", 10)])
survey("core: 4 P routers + 2 dual-homed PEs", core, msd=3)

r = ring8.repair("C", "E", ("link", "C", "D"))
print("\nWorked case: 8-node ring, PLR C, destination E, protect link C-D")
print("  primary path   ", " -> ".join(ring8.path("C", "E")[0]))
print("  post-converge  ", " -> ".join(r["pc"]), f"(cost {r['cost']})")
print("  P on path      ", r["P"], " Q on path", r["Q"], " kind:", r["kind"])
print("  repair list    ", ", ".join(fmt_seg(ring8, s) for s in r["segs"]), "| out via", r["nexthop"])
print("  label stack    ", ring8.labels(r, "E"), "top first")
print("  LFA? ", lfa_ok(ring8, "C", "E", "D"), "  remote LFA?", lfa_ok(ring8, "C", "E", "D") or rlfa_ok(ring8, "C", "E", ("link", "C", "D")))
```

`lfa_ok` is the RFC 5286 link-protection test: a neighbour N other than the primary next hop is a loop-free alternate for D if dist(N, D) < dist(N, S) + dist(S, D), meaning N's own shortest path to D does not come back through S. `rlfa_ok` is the remote LFA condition from RFC 7490: there is some node in both S's extended P-space and D's Q-space, to which S could tunnel the packet. Remote LFA as deployed uses a targeted LDP session to that PQ node; with SR the same node is reached with one Node-SID.

```text
== 6-node ring, all metrics 10: 6 nodes, link protection, 30 (PLR, destination) pairs
  LFA (RFC 5286)        6/30 (20%)
  LFA + remote LFA      30/30 (100%)
  TI-LFA (RFC 9855)     30/30 (100%)
  SR labels on the repaired packet: 1 labels: 6, 2 labels: 24
  pairs over MSD 3: 0  (deepest TI-LFA stack 2; Adj-SID-only would need up to 5)
== 6-node ring, F-A metric 100: 6 nodes, link protection, 30 (PLR, destination) pairs
  LFA (RFC 5286)        10/30 (33%)
  LFA + remote LFA      10/30 (33%)
  TI-LFA (RFC 9855)     30/30 (100%)
  SR labels on the repaired packet: 0 labels: 2, 1 labels: 12, 2 labels: 14, 3 labels: 2
  pairs over MSD 3: 0  (deepest TI-LFA stack 3; Adj-SID-only would need up to 5)
== 8-node ring, H-A metric 100: 8 nodes, link protection, 56 (PLR, destination) pairs

  SR labels on the repaired packet: 0 labels: 2, 1 labels: 16, 2 labels: 26, 3 labels: 12
  over MSD 2: PLR C -> D, link C-D: 3 labels [16001, 24101, 16004] via C -> B -> A -> H -> G -> F -> E -> D
  over MSD 2: PLR C -> E, link C-D: 3 labels [16001, 24101, 16005] via C -> B -> A -> H -> G -> F -> E
  over MSD 2: PLR C -> F, link C-D: 3 labels [16001, 24101, 16006] via C -> B -> A -> H -> G -> F
  pairs over MSD 2: 12  (deepest TI-LFA stack 3; Adj-SID-only would need up to 7)
== core: 4 P routers + 2 dual-homed PEs: 6 nodes, link protection, 30 (PLR, destination) pairs

Worked case: 8-node ring, PLR C, destination E, protect link C-D
  primary path    C -> D -> E
  post-converge   C -> B -> A -> H -> G -> F -> E (cost 150)
  P on path       ['A', 'B', 'C']  Q on path ['E', 'F', 'G', 'H']  kind: P and Q adjacent (Node-SID + Adj-SID)
  repair list     Node-SID(A)=16001, Adj-SID(A-H)=24101 | out via B
  label stack     [16001, 24101, 16005] top first
```

## Reading the results

**Rings are where plain LFA fails.** On the six-node ring with equal metrics, only 6 of 30 (PLR, destination) pairs have an LFA. In an even ring, a neighbour's shortest path to most destinations runs back through the PLR. Remote LFA fixes all of them: there is always a node half-way round that is in both spaces.

**One expensive span breaks remote LFA too.** Give one link of the same ring metric 100 (a long-haul span, or a link someone costed out) and remote LFA adds nothing over LFA: 10 of 30 either way. The expensive span pushes the P-space and Q-space apart so that no single node is in both. TI-LFA still covers all 30, and two of the repairs need three labels.

**Bigger rings make deeper stacks.** On the eight-node ring with one costly span, TI-LFA again covers 56 of 56, but 12 pairs need three labels. The printed examples are all PLR C losing link C-D: the post-convergence path goes the whole way round, C, B, A, H and on. A is the deepest node C can reach on old paths without crossing C-D, and H is the first node whose own path to the destination avoids C-D. Pinning the costly A-H link takes Node-SID(A) and Adj-SID(A-H), and the destination's label sits underneath. If this PLR could only push two labels, those 12 pairs would be unprotected. Pinning every hop with Adj-SIDs instead would need up to seven.

**Well-meshed cores barely need SR.** The four-router core with two dual-homed PEs has 100% LFA coverage and every repair is a plain swap toward a different next hop (one label: the destination's). That matches field experience: TI-LFA's value shows on rings, long chains and sparse regional networks, not on dense fabrics. Run the coverage numbers on your own topology before arguing about it.

**The worked case.** The last block is C protecting link C-D toward E on the eight-node ring. Neither LFA nor remote LFA works. TI-LFA sends the packet to B with labels `[16001, 24101, 16005]`: B forwards on A's Node-SID (and pops it, being A's penultimate hop under PHP), A pops its own Adj-SID 24101 and sends the packet over A-H, and H forwards on E's label along H, G, F, E. When C's own SPF finishes, C installs the post-convergence route and the repair is withdrawn; because the repair already followed that path, traffic does not move.

## TI-LFA in FRR (not run here)

Not run here: written from the FRR `isisd` and `ospfd` documentation. Use it on a lab host with the Linux MPLS modules (`mpls_router`, `mpls_iptunnel`) loaded and `net.mpls.platform_labels` and per-interface `net.mpls.conf.<ifname>.input` set, for example in Containerlab with FRR nodes.

```text
! not run here: IS-IS with SR-MPLS and TI-LFA on one router
router isis CORE
 net 49.0001.0000.0000.0001.00
 is-type level-2-only
 segment-routing on
 segment-routing global-block 16000 23999
 segment-routing node-msd 8
 segment-routing prefix 10.255.0.1/32 index 1
!
interface eth1
 ip router isis CORE
 isis network point-to-point
 isis fast-reroute ti-lfa level-2
!
interface eth2
 ip router isis CORE
 isis network point-to-point
 isis fast-reroute ti-lfa level-2 node-protection link-fallback
```

```text
! not run here: OSPF equivalent (protection is configured per instance)
router ospf
 segment-routing on
 segment-routing global-block 16000 23999
 segment-routing node-msd 8
 segment-routing prefix 10.255.0.1/32 index 1
 fast-reroute ti-lfa
```

Commands to compare against the model (not run here):

```text
show isis route level-2 backup
show isis route level-2 prefix-sid
show isis fast-reroute summary level-2
show isis segment-routing node
show mpls table
```

`show isis route ... backup` lists the backup next hop and the label stack per prefix. Feed the same topology and metrics into `tilfa.py` and compare. Differences usually come from one of: a different tie-break among equal-cost post-convergence paths, the implementation shortening the P-to-Q stretch with an extra Node-SID, node protection versus link protection, or a non-uniform SRGB.

## Gotchas

1. **Equal-cost paths shrink P-space.** A node reachable over two equal paths, one through X, is not in P-space. The RFC 9855 Figure 1 text is loose on this; the lab shows the strict result and why the extended P-space still finds R1. If your mental calculation disagrees with the router, check for ECMP first.
2. **Node protection needs more labels than link protection.** Protecting against F's failure removes all of F's links, so the post-convergence path is longer and Q is further away. Some platforms fall back to link protection if no node-protecting repair fits (FRR's `link-fallback` keyword).
3. **MSD is per platform, and per line card.** A repair the IGP happily computes is useless if the hardware cannot push it. Watch for "unprotected" counters in the FRR summary and vendor equivalents after enabling node protection.
4. **Non-uniform SRGBs change labels mid-path.** Rule 2 re-pushes the active segment with the label from *Q's* SRGB. With different SRGBs per router, a label that is correct at S is wrong at Q. Keep one SRGB network-wide unless you have a migration reason.
5. **PHP decides whether the destination label is on the packet.** The same repair can be three or four labels depending on the no-PHP and explicit-null flags of the destination's Node-SID. Count both when sizing MSD.
6. **The repair is only as fast as detection.** TI-LFA is precomputed, but it starts when S notices the failure. Loss of light is fast; a silent failure behind a media converter needs BFD.
7. **Microloops are a separate problem.** TI-LFA protects traffic until S converges. Other routers converge in a different order and can loop briefly. Microloop avoidance (RFC 8333 for local convergence) and ordered updates are complementary.
8. **Policies and Flex-Algo.** TI-LFA follows IGP shortest paths. Traffic on an SR Policy or a Flexible Algorithm may be repaired off its constraint unless the implementation computes repairs per algorithm (RFC 9855 section 8).
9. **SRLGs are invisible to plain SPF.** Two links in the same conduit fail together. Without SRLG-aware TI-LFA, the computed repair can use the other link in the same duct.

## Exercises

1. In `rfc-figures.py`, change the S-N1 metric from 1 to 2 so that S's paths to R1 no longer tie. Rerun and check that R1 now appears in the plain P(S, N1). Does the RL change?
2. Switch Figure 1 to link protection (`("link", "S", "N1")`) instead of node protection. Compare the post-convergence path and RL. Why is the repair so much shorter?
3. In `coverage.py`, add a chord (for example C-G with metric 30) to the eight-node ring. How do LFA, remote LFA and the label-depth histogram change? Which pairs drop below MSD 2?
4. Add a `node` mode to `survey` that protects the primary next-hop *node* instead of the link (skip destinations that are that node). Compare the share of three-label repairs on the eight-node ring with link protection.
5. Model a non-uniform SRGB: give node H a base of 20000 and change `labels()` so the re-pushed destination label uses Q's base. Print the stack for the worked case and explain which router reads which label.
6. Pick one repair from the eight-node ring and walk the packet hop by hop, writing the label stack at each router (push, swap, pop, PHP). Confirm that no router on the way forwards back toward C-D.
